idiom_name: select(...).with_for_update(nowait=True, skip_locked=True) inside a session transaction
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy 2.0 makes the pessimistic read explicit: select(LockRecord).where(...).with_for_update(nowait=True, skip_locked=True) emits FOR UPDATE with the backend's NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED, and the documentation recommends populate_existing() so the identity map cannot return a stale object. The lock ends at commit, so the offline lease is the lock record's owner/timeout columns; with_for_update() is also documented as unsupported and discouraged together with joined eager loading, hence the lock record is loaded in its own query rather than joined to the data it protects.
code_sketch:
with Session(engine) as session, session.begin():        # short transaction
    lock = session.execute(
        select(LockRecord)
        .where(LockRecord.lockable == key)
        .with_for_update(nowait=True)
        .execution_options(populate_existing=True)
    ).scalar_one_or_none()
    if lock is None:
        session.add(LockRecord(lockable=key, owner=session_id))
    elif lock.owner != session_id:
        raise Locked(lock.owner)
pitfalls: The identity map can hand back a stale LockRecord even while the row is locked - populate_existing() is what makes the read trustworthy, as the documentation warns.
with_for_update() combined with joined eager loading locks every involved table and is explicitly not supported/recommended; take the lock in its own query.
A lock acquired on a session that is then closed or committed is released immediately, so never treat session.begin() as the offline lease.

variants.name: PostgreSQL advisory locks as the lease
variants.idiom_name: pg_advisory_lock / pg_advisory_xact_lock instead of a lock table
variants.implementation_notes: On PostgreSQL the lock table can be replaced by advisory locks: pg_advisory_xact_lock releases itself at the end of the claiming transaction, while a session-level pg_advisory_lock survives transactions and is released only explicitly or when the session ends - the closest thing to a server-managed offline lease. The price is that the lease lives on one database connection: the application must pin a connection per editing session and close it on logout, and no business row records who holds what. Choose this variant for short, high-frequency claims; keep the lock table when visibility, timeouts and administrative release matter.
variants.code_sketch:
con = engine.raw_connection()          # pinned for the whole edit session
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(%s)", (key_hash,))
# ... requests read and update the aggregate; other sessions block here
try:
    handle_requests(con)
finally:
    cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(%s)", (key_hash,))
pitfalls: Session-level advisory locks ignore transaction semantics: a rollback does not release them, and there is no explicit unlock for the transaction-level variant - mixing the two leaks locks (PostgreSQL documents this asymmetry).
Advisory locks are invisible in business tables: an administrator cannot delete a stale lock, only find the holding session in pg_locks and terminate it.
A pooled connection checkout is not a session: if the connection goes back to the pool the lock survives on that connection and blocks whoever gets the same slot next.
